title: YOU CAN LOVE JESUS AND STILL BE IN LOVE WITH THE WORLD
paragraphs: YOU CAN LOVE JESUS AND STILL BE IN LOVE WITH THE WORLD

“Do not love the world” does not mean what many people think it means. John was not telling you to stop loving people, beauty, laughter, work, family, or the life God gave you. He was exposing something far more dangerous: a rival love that can quietly occupy the throne of your heart while your lips still say, “Jesus.”
There is a frightening kind of distance from God that does not look like distance.
You can still pray.
Still open your Bible.
Still know the worship songs.
Still post the verse.
Still say, “God is good.”
And somewhere beneath all of that, something else can slowly become more precious to you than God Himself.
Approval.
Money.
Attention.
Sexual desire.
Comfort.
Success.
Status.
Being admired.
Being right.
Being wanted.
Being noticed.
Even the desperate need to prove that your life matters.
Nothing may look scandalous from the outside.
But inside, another kingdom may be competing for your affection.
That is why the apostle John wrote words that can sound almost severe:
“Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world.” — 1 John 2:15
But if we misunderstand what John means by “world,” we can misunderstand the entire warning.
The Greek text begins:
Μὴ ἀγαπᾶτε τὸν κόσμον μηδὲ τὰ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ.
Mē agapate ton kosmon mēde ta en tō kosmō.
“Do not love the world, nor the things in the world.”
The crucial word is κόσμος — kosmos.
And this is where context matters.
Because the Bible also says:
“For God so loved the world…” — John 3:16
So which is it?
God loves the world, but Christians must not love the world?
Is Scripture contradicting itself?
No.

The same Greek word can carry different shades of meaning depending upon context. Kosmos can refer to the created world, humanity, or the ordered system of human existence. In 1 John 2, John immediately explains the particular “world” he is warning us not to love.
He writes:
There it is.
John is not commanding you to hate the planet God created.
He is not commanding you to stop loving unbelievers.
He is certainly not giving Christians permission to withdraw into religious superiority and look down upon everyone outside the church.
Jesus Himself destroys that interpretation.

God loved the world enough to give His Son for sinners (John 3:16). Jesus came “to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10). He ate with people religious society considered scandalous (Luke 5:29–32). He commanded His followers to love even their enemies (Matthew 5:44).
The “world” John warns against is the rebellious order of desire, pride, self-rule, and misplaced affection that operates in opposition to the Father.
It is humanity arranging life as though God were unnecessary.
It is creation enjoyed while the Creator is ignored.
It is receiving God's gifts and then allowing those gifts to replace God.
And suddenly this verse becomes uncomfortable.
Because “the world” is not merely somewhere outside the church doors.
The battlefield can be inside us.
John describes three dimensions of this rival kingdom.
He speaks of ἡ ἐπιθυμία τῆς σαρκός — hē epithymia tēs sarkos, “the desire of the flesh.”
Then ἡ ἐπιθυμία τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν — hē epithymia tōn ophthalmōn, “the desire of the eyes.”
And finally ἡ ἀλαζονεία τοῦ βίου — hē alazoneia tou biou, often translated “the pride of life.”
Our flesh says:
I need to feel it.
Our eyes say:
I need to have it.
Our pride says:
I need people to know I have it.
And the world has become extraordinarily skilled at feeding all three.
Scroll.
Compare.
Want.
Envy.
Perform.
Buy.
Display.
Repeat.
Someone else's marriage looks happier.
Someone else's body looks better.
Someone else's ministry grows faster.
Someone else's children seem more successful.
Someone else's house is larger.
Someone else's career is advancing.
Someone else's post gets thousands of reactions while yours disappears unnoticed.
And without ever formally renouncing Christ, the heart can begin living for the approval of people Christ died to free us from needing.
That is how subtle worldliness can be.
It does not always arrive carrying a bottle, walking into a nightclub, or announcing some spectacular rebellion.
Sometimes worldliness walks into church carrying a Bible.
Sometimes it preaches.
Sometimes it sings worship songs.
Sometimes it knows Christian vocabulary perfectly.
Sometimes it wants the platform more than the presence of God.
Sometimes it wants to be known as holy more than it actually wants holiness.
Sometimes it wants Jesus because Jesus might improve its life, not because Jesus is Lord.
And sometimes it whispers:
If nobody sees what I do, does it still matter?
Jesus answered that question long before social media existed.
Your Father sees in secret.
Matthew 6 repeats that truth when Jesus warns against practicing righteousness merely to be seen by others.
That means there is a kind of Christianity that can appear deeply spiritual while secretly feeding on human applause.
The issue is not whether people see you.
The issue is whether being seen has become your reward.
That distinction can hurt.
Because some of us are exhausted not because obedience to Christ is exhausting, but because maintaining an image is exhausting.
You are trying to look healed while still bleeding.
Trying to look strong while privately collapsing.
Trying to look faithful while temptation is eating you alive.
Trying to convince everyone that your marriage is fine.
Trying to convince everyone that your faith is fine.
Maybe trying to convince yourself.
And Jesus is not standing over you waiting for your performance to improve.
He is calling you out of hiding.
There is a difference.
The Gospel is not God telling broken people to become impressive enough for Him.
The Gospel is God coming for sinners who could never rescue themselves.
That is why “Do not love the world” cannot be separated from grace.
John is not saying, “Stop loving the world so God might finally love you.”
The Gospel says something far more astonishing.
God loved sinners first.
“We love him, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).
The order matters.
Grace comes first.
Then transformed affection.
Christ does not merely hand us a list of forbidden loves.
He gives us a greater Love.
And when Jesus becomes more beautiful to the heart, the cheap substitutes begin losing their power.
Not instantly in every struggle.
Not without warfare.
Not without repentance.
Not without falling sometimes and getting back up.
But genuinely.
This is why Christianity is deeper than behavior modification.
You can remove a sinful behavior while still worshiping the desire underneath it.
A person can stop chasing sexual immorality and begin chasing religious admiration.
Stop worshiping money and start worshiping ministry success.
Stop getting drunk on alcohol and become intoxicated with attention.
Stop seeking acceptance at the club and start seeking acceptance in the church.
The idol changes clothes.
The throne remains occupied.
Jesus wants the throne.
And He has every right to it.
He did not purchase you cheaply.
The cross tells us what our rescue cost.
The eternal Son of God took on flesh. Christ lived without sin. He went willingly to the cross. He bore judgment for sinners. He died. He was buried. He rose bodily from the grave.
The Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is rescue.
And maybe that is why this subject hurts so much.
Because somewhere inside us, we know.
We know what we keep reaching for when God feels distant.
We know whose approval can control our mood.
We know what we would be terrified to lose.
We know the secret browser history.
The private fantasy.
The resentment.
The obsession with money.
The hunger for recognition.
The relationship we know is pulling us away from Christ.
The compromise we renamed so we would not have to repent of it.
We know.
And still Jesus calls.
Not because sin does not matter.
Precisely because it does.
Repentance is not Jesus humiliating you.
Repentance is Jesus calling you away from something that is killing what He intends to make alive.

The Greek word commonly translated “repent” in the New Testament, μετανοέω — metanoeō, carries the idea of changing one's mind or turning in response to truth. Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt remorse.
Peter wept bitterly.
But Peter returned to Christ.
The Gospel does not merely expose.
It restores.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Think about the scandal of that.
He had walked with Christ.
He had seen miracles.
He had confessed Him as the Christ.
He had promised loyalty.
Then, under pressure, Peter denied even knowing Him.
And Jesus knew Peter would do it.
Yet after the resurrection, Jesus came for him.
John 21 gives us one of Scripture's most tender restoration scenes.
Peter, the man who failed publicly, stands before the risen Christ.
Jesus does not pretend the failure never happened.
He goes directly to the heart:
“Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these?”
Love.
That was the issue.
Not image.
Not reputation.
Not Peter proving he deserved another opportunity.
Love.
“Do you love Me?”
And the man whose story could have ended in shame was restored and recommissioned by Jesus.
That is the Gospel Warrior theme written across the pages of Scripture.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by pretending sin never happened.
Jesus rewrites the sinner's future by dealing truthfully and decisively with sin through His cross, forgiving those who come to Him, and transforming those who belong to Him.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace opens the prison door.
So ask yourself a question that may be harder than asking whether you believe in God.
What does your heart run toward when nobody is watching?
What gives you identity?
What destroys your peace when you cannot have it?
What are you afraid Jesus might ask you to surrender?
What could God remove from your life that would make you feel as though life itself were no longer worth living?
Sometimes our strongest emotional reaction reveals where an idol has buried its roots.
And perhaps right now, you already know what yours is.
Do not run from that conviction.
Run with it to Christ.
There is no freedom in hiding from the One who already knows.
Hebrews 4:13 tells us that nothing is hidden from His sight.
But the next verses do not leave us trembling at a locked door.
Because we have a great High Priest—Jesus, the Son of God.
And Hebrews 4:16 therefore calls us to come boldly to the throne of grace to receive mercy and find grace in time of need.
Did you catch that?
The God from whom you cannot hide is also the God who invites repentant sinners to a throne called grace.
That changes everything.
You do not have to clean the blood off yourself before approaching the Physician.
Come.
Confess it.
Name it.
Stop protecting it.
Stop renaming it.
Stop blaming everyone else for it.
Stop saying, “That's just how I am.”
Bring it into the light.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Notice that John does not say God is merely sentimental about forgiveness.
He says God is faithful and just to forgive.
For the Christian, forgiveness rests ultimately on Christ's finished work.
Jesus paid for sin.
That is why grace is infinitely more serious than pretending sin does not matter.
At Calvary, sin mattered enough for Christ to die.
And sinners mattered enough for Him to go willingly.
So when John says, “Do not love the world,” he is not trying to make your life smaller.
He is calling you out of slavery to things too small to satisfy you.
Because then comes the line we desperately need in an age obsessed with what is temporary:
“And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.” — 1 John 2:17
The Greek contains the verb παράγεται — paragetai.
The world is passing away.
Passing.
Away.
The face you are desperately trying to keep young.
Passing.
The possessions you are accumulating.
Passing.
The applause.
Passing.
The followers.
Passing.
The title beside your name.
Passing.
The numbers in your bank account.
Passing.
The house.
Passing.
The car.
Passing.
The trends.
Passing.
The people whose approval currently feels indispensable.
Passing.
One day, somebody else will live in houses we fought to own.
Somebody else will possess things we sacrificed years to buy.
Names once celebrated will become names nobody recognizes.
Our bodies will return to dust unless Christ returns first.
And standing before God, none of us will wish we had spent more of our lives trying to impress strangers.
This is not an argument for abandoning work, possessions, ambition, creativity, or enjoyment.

Scripture can speak positively about receiving God's gifts with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4–5), working wholeheartedly unto the Lord (Colossians 3:23), and God richly providing things to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17).
The problem is not possessing something.
The problem begins when something possesses you.
Enjoy the gift.
Worship the Giver.
Love people.
Use possessions.
Never reverse those two.
And perhaps that is the simplest way to understand “Do not love the world.”
Do not give temporary things the love that belongs ultimately to the eternal God.
Do not ask creation to carry the weight only the Creator can bear.
Do not make another human being your savior.
Do not make money your security.
Do not make attention your oxygen.
Do not make pleasure your god.
Do not make success your identity.
Do not make your failure your identity either.
Your worst chapter does not have authority greater than the blood of Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have been worldly.
Maybe spectacularly so.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe your scandal became public.
Maybe yours remained buried beneath Sunday clothes and practiced smiles.
The invitation is still Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
Jesus Christ is not merely offering you a cleaner public image.
He offers reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness.
A new heart.
A new allegiance.
A new direction.
A new life.
This is why the Gospel is not, “Try harder so God will tolerate you.”

It is the announcement that salvation is found in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again, and that those who turn to Him in repentance and faith receive what they could never earn for themselves.
Grace.
And grace begins rewriting people.
From lust to purity.
From greed to generosity.
From pride to humility.
From bitterness to forgiveness.
From performance to surrender.
From hiding to confession.
From death to life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn this moment into another piece of Christian content you consume and forget.
Be honest.
There may be another believer reading the comments who needs to discover that they are not the only person fighting.
Your honesty may become somebody else's courage.
And if one person came to mind while you were reading this, do not ignore that.
Let them see the cross.
Let them see grace.
Let them see Jesus.
Because the world will start preaching to you again tomorrow.
Probably within minutes.
You will be told again that you need more to matter.
More attention.
More money.
More beauty.
More approval.
More things.
More applause.
Come back and remember:
The world is passing away. Jesus is not.

Following Gospel Warrior also helps you stay connected to daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment. Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even unbelievers—to follow along. You never know which truth God may use to awaken a heart.
Who has your love?
Not merely your church attendance.
Not your Christian vocabulary.
Not your public identity.
Your love.
Because eventually everything we built our lives around will reveal whether it could bear the weight of our souls.
The world says, “Love me, and I will give you everything.”
Then it takes everything and eventually leaves you with nothing.
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
And though following Him costs us the right to rule ourselves, in Him we discover the life the world could never manufacture.
So release what is passing.
Cling to the One who remains.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the appetite you cannot seem to control.
Bring Him the ambition.
Bring Him the broken relationship.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the addiction to approval.
Bring Him the version of yourself you are exhausted from pretending to be.
Bring Him even the scandal.
Especially the scandal.
Because the cross has already proven that Jesus is not afraid to enter the ugliest chapter of a human story.
And the empty tomb has already proven that He specializes in endings death never saw coming.
Because someday the thing you thought you could never live without will be gone.
Make sure the One you cannot live without is the One who will never pass away.
